reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / AAO Basic and Clinical Science Course
clinicalPearls: A small, discrete, usually congenital opacity at the anterior pole of the lens involving the capsule and immediate subcapsular cortex, commonly bilateral and frequently non-progressive
Most are visually insignificant and axial, allowing good vision, so many are managed by observation rather than surgery
A pyramidal variant projects forward into the anterior chamber as a small cone and is more likely to be visually consequential
Familial cases are often inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so examining relatives can be informative
Even a small opacity can be amblyogenic in a child through induced astigmatism or light scatter, so cycloplegic refraction and amblyopia monitoring are essential
Recognised associations include persistent pupillary membrane, microphthalmos, anterior lenticonus and anterior segment dysgenesis such as Peters anomaly
It is thought to reflect a developmental disturbance in the separation of the lens vesicle from the surface ectoderm, with focal anterior epithelial proliferation
Surgery is reserved for opacities dense or large enough to threaten vision or drive amblyopia, with attention to a normal posterior capsule during lens removal
reference.pathophysiology: During embryogenesis the lens vesicle detaches from the overlying surface ectoderm; an anterior polar cataract is believed to result from incomplete or abnormal separation, leaving a focus of aberrant anterior lens epithelium that proliferates and produces a localised capsular and subcapsular opacity. In the pyramidal form, continued abnormal epithelial and fibrous growth extends the opacity anteriorly into the aqueous. The lesion is typically stationary because it is a fixed developmental scar, although the surrounding cortex remains clear. Associated anterior segment maldevelopment, as in Peters anomaly or persistent pupillary membrane, reflects the shared window of anterior segment morphogenesis in which the insult occurs.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior subcapsular cataract of acquired or inflammatory origin
Peters anomaly and other anterior segment dysgenesis
Persistent pupillary membrane adherent to the lens
Corneal opacity or leukoma projected onto the lens plane
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy to localise the opacity to the anterior capsule and note any pyramidal projection
Cycloplegic refraction and keratometry to detect associated astigmatism and anisometropia
Age-appropriate visual acuity and fixation testing to screen for amblyopia in children
Retro-illumination and red reflex assessment to gauge the visual significance of the opacity
Examination for anterior segment dysgenesis, persistent pupillary membrane and microphthalmos
Examination of parents and siblings where a familial (autosomal dominant) pattern is suspected
redFlags: A dense or enlarging axial opacity in an infant at high risk of deprivation amblyopia
Associated features of anterior segment dysgenesis such as Peters anomaly with corneal involvement and glaucoma risk
Significant anisometropia or high astigmatism threatening binocular development
Rapid change in an opacity previously thought stationary, prompting review of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Most anterior polar cataracts are stationary and visually insignificant, carrying an excellent prognosis with observation alone. When the opacity is large, pyramidal or associated with significant refractive error, the outlook depends on prompt correction of ametropia and treatment of amblyopia, and on the presence of any co-existing anterior segment anomaly.
pitfalls: Assuming all anterior polar cataracts are harmless and missing amblyopia from induced astigmatism
Overlooking associated anterior segment dysgenesis and its glaucoma risk
Proceeding to unnecessary surgery for a stable, visually insignificant opacity
Neglecting refractive correction and occlusion in favour of watching the opacity alone
Failing to counsel families about the dominant inheritance and to examine relatives
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
